analysis.one_liner: Adds 20 years to copyright terms, keeping books, music, and films out of the public domain longer.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; introduced with zero cosponsors, it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added 20 years to nearly every copyright term: works by individual authors would stay locked up for the author's life plus 70 years instead of 50, and works made for hire would stay private for 95 years instead of 75. It would also extend federal protection for sound recordings made before 1972 all the way to 2067. In exchange, it offered libraries a narrow right to preserve works in their final 20 years of copyright, and restored some authors' ability to reclaim old licenses.
analysis.who_benefits: Copyright owners — record labels, movie studios, book publishers, and heirs of long-dead authors — would gain 20 more years of exclusive control over works that already exist, letting them keep charging for reprints, reissues, and streaming without competition. Owners of old recordings (pre-1972) would get protection extended to 2067. A separate provision would let some authors and their heirs terminate old contracts and take back rights from publishers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Record labels, studios, and copyright holders
analysis.who_pays: Everyone who reads, listens, or builds on the past. Works that would have entered the public domain — becoming free to copy, reprint, translate, adapt, or stream — would stay locked up for two more decades. Libraries, archives, teachers, small publishers, and independent creators would keep paying license fees or go without, and the original authors would mostly not benefit because they are dead.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, libraries, and reusing creators
analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs far outweigh the benefits for the public. Extending terms on works that already exist gives the original creators nothing — they are dead or long finished — while delaying by 20 years the moment their work becomes freely available. The bill's own offsets are small: the library exception applies only to works in their last 20 years that are not being commercially exploited, and the author termination right, while genuinely valuable to a few songwriters and their heirs, applies only to pre-1978 contracts. As designed, the bill is a long extension of private monopoly control with modest carve-outs.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee sent it to its intellectual property subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, libraries, archives, educators, and anyone who reuses or builds on older works kept access they would have lost for another 20 years; copyright owners did not get the extension from this bill.

for.name: Sonny Bono
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Copyright Term Extension Act and shepherded the referral to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Recording and motion picture copyright industries
for.role: Industries seeking longer exclusive rights over catalogs and old recordings
for.what_they_did: Backed longer copyright terms covering sound recordings and long-lived works, the policy this bill embodies.

against.name: Subcommittee on Courts and Intellectual Property
against.role: House Judiciary subcommittee with jurisdiction over copyright
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 29, 1997 and never took it up; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without scheduling any action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes or recorded opposition, so the partisan shape of this bill's fate cannot be measured; its sole sponsor was a Republican with no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would extend federal protection for sound recordings made before 1972 to 2067 and add 20 years to music copyright terms, keeping old recordings under exclusive control and off the public domain. Their gain is paid for by listeners, libraries, and companies that would reissue or stream those recordings.

industries.industry: Motion picture studios and holders of long-lived franchises
industries.note: Longer terms for works made for hire (95 years from publication) keep classic films and characters exclusively controlled for decades longer. The public pays through continued licensed-only access and delayed free reuse.
The extension locks up books for two more decades, letting publishers and heirs keep exclusive reprint and licensing rights on works whose creators are mostly deceased.

The bill would give libraries a new right to preserve and share works digitally during each work's final 20 years of copyright, but only when the work is not commercially exploited and no copy is reasonably available. That small gain comes alongside the much larger loss of public-domain material the extension would lock away.
